na2b7a9c6efd5: Electrocardiographic analysis aided by artificial intelligence (AI) may identify atrial electrical vulnerability during sinus rhythm. The objective of this study was to determine whether AI–enabled ECG (AI-ECG) is effective for detecting atrial fibrillation (AF), atrial flutter (AFl), or prespecified pre-AF atrial findings in a randomized trial. In this single-center, open-label trial, 14 665 adults 40 to 85 years of age without previous AF/AFl were randomized to an AI-ECG–guided strategy or usual care. Participants randomized to AI-ECG who were then identified by AI as having a high-risk sinus-rhythm ECG in the preceding year were offered Holter monitoring for ≤7 days. Each monitored high-risk intervention participant was paired with an age- and sex-matched control selected before control ECGs underwent AI analysis. Matched controls received identical monitoring to reduce ascertainment bias. Reporting cardiologists were blinded to AI results and randomized assignment. The primary outcome was a composite of newly detected AF, AFl, or pre-AF atrial findings within 90 days. Pre-AF atrial findings comprised frequent premature atrial complexes, short runs of premature atrial complexes, or nonsustained AF/AFl. Among 7337 intervention and 7328 control participants, 84 (1.1%) and 78 (1.1%), respectively, were classified as high risk. Of the 84 high-risk intervention participants, 48 (57.1%) underwent monitoring, as did 48 matched controls. The primary outcome occurred in 54 intervention participants (0.74%) versus 35 control participants (0.48%; odds ratio, 1.54 [95% CI, 1.01–2.37]; P =0.046). Hypothetical reclassification of 1 intervention event to a nonevent changed the primary analysis P value to 0.057. The intervention effect on detection of the primary composite outcome differed by baseline AI-ECG risk ( P interaction <0.001): 32.1% versus 2.6% among high-risk participants and 0.4% versus 0.5% among low-risk participants. AF/AFl detection (0.3% versus 0.2%) and antiarrhythmic therapy initiation at 180 days (2.3% versus 2.4%) did not differ significantly between the intervention and control groups. Participant-reported monitoring-related adverse events, including skin reactions and discomfort, occurred in 22.9% of monitored intervention participants versus 18.8% of matched controls. AI-ECG–guided monitoring resulted in a modest increase in the detection of new AF, AFl, or pre-AF atrial findings. However, these findings were fragile statistically and sensitive to reclassification of 1 event. LATENT (Leveraging AI-ECG Technology for Early Notification and Tracking of AF Development) demonstrates the clinical application of AI-ECG risk stratification to guide targeted rhythm surveillance, providing a foundation for larger trials evaluating its impact on patient outcomes. URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT06847932.
n7f25bc092a25: In the ISCHEMIA-CKD trial (International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness With Medical and Invasive Approaches–Chronic Kidney Disease), at a median follow-up of 2.2 years, the primary composite outcome of death or nonfatal myocardial infarction was similar between an initial invasive strategy (INV) compared with an initial conservative strategy (CON) in patients with moderate or severe myocardial ischemia and advanced chronic kidney disease. However, the long-term outcomes comparing the 2 strategies are unknown. Participants in the ISCHEMIA-CKD trial were randomly assigned to either INV, involving coronary angiography and revascularization when feasible, added to guideline-directed medical therapy or to CON with guideline-directed medical therapy alone and invasive procedures reserved for failure of guideline-directed medical therapy. After the active intervention trial phase, long-term vital status follow-up was conducted through participant contact by participating sites and by health record and centralized death database searches. The primary outcome for the extended follow-up phase was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes were cause-specific mortality, including cardiovascular and noncardiovascular mortality. Among the 777 participants randomized (388 to INV and 389 to CON), over a median of 8 years of follow-up, vital status retention among survivors was 95%. There was a total of 429 deaths (55%). Cumulative all-cause mortality (57.4% versus 56.8%; adjusted hazard ratio, 1.05 [95% CI, 0.87–1.28]) or cardiovascular mortality (40.3% versus 38.4%; adjusted hazard ratio, 1.06 [95% CI, 0.84–1.34]) at 8 years did not differ between INV and CON. The restricted mean survival time was 1941 days (1834–2047 days) for INV versus 1990 days (1885–2094 days) for CON, with an adjusted estimated difference of −99 days (−245 to 46). The posterior probability of at least a 1 percentage point lower or higher death with INV at the 8-year median follow-up was 28% and 52%, respectively. Similarly, the posterior probability of at least a 1 percentage point lower or higher cardiovascular mortality with INV was 23% and 56%, respectively. In patients with at least moderate ischemia and advanced chronic kidney disease, there was no significant long-term benefit of an initial INV at reducing the risk of all-cause or cardiovascular mortality compared with an initial conservative strategy. n30b9e7a99541: Background: In acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS), the myocardium sustains a dual injury: ischemia of the culprit territory and global hypoperfusion from low cardiac output. Whether platelet inhibition at reperfusion affects the microcirculation, the infarct, the noninfarcted myocardium, and ventricular function, and over what time course, has not been examined with serial imaging. The prespecified multimodality imaging substudy of the randomized DAPT-SHOCK-AMI trial (intravenous cangrelor versus crushed oral ticagrelor) addressed this question. Methods: Patients at prespecified imaging sites underwent serial echocardiography (208 enrolled; evaluable examinations in 175, 120, and 99 patients in the acute phase, at 1 month, and at 1 year) and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR; 93 enrolled; 73, 68, and 63); 81 patients (40 and 41) underwent both modalities. Blinded core laboratories analyzed all studies. The primary imaging endpoint was microvascular obstruction (MVO) on acute CMR, evaluable in 60 patients; secondary endpoints were infarct size, native T1 of the global, infarcted, and remote myocardium, left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), E/e', and left atrial volume, and their changes. Comparisons between the cangrelor and crushed ticagrelor arms used covariate-adjusted logistic or linear regression; the substudy was not separately powered. Results: The odds of acute MVO were lower with cangrelor (adjusted odds ratio 0.27 [95% CI 0.08 to 0.98]; P=0.023). Infarct size did not differ between the arms. At 1 year, native T1 of the remote myocardium was lower with cangrelor (adjusted mean 1114 [95% CI 1057 to 1171] versus 1171 [1115 to 1228] ms; P=0.005). Over 1 year, LVEF increased more with cangrelor on echocardiography (37.9% versus 21.7% of the acute value; adjusted P=0.046) and CMR (15.8% versus 2.1%; P=0.027), with greater improvement in GLS, lower E/e', and less left atrial enlargement; no parameter differed between the arms at 1 month. Conclusions: In AMI-CS, serial multimodality imaging characterized microvascular, tissue-level, and functional injury over 1 year. Cangrelor was associated with less acute MVO, lower remote native T1, and more complete recovery of LV function than crushed ticagrelor, without a difference in infarct size; these hypothesis-generating findings suggest differences in the microcirculation and non-infarcted myocardial injury but do not establish a treatment mechanism.
nede841bebfd1: In a target-directed low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)–lowering strategy, the impact of the initial treatment regimen has not been investigated in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. We compared the efficacy and safety of initial statin–ezetimibe combination therapy versus statin monotherapy within intensive or conventional LDL-C–targeting strategies. In this prespecified second randomization of the randomized Ez-PAVE trial (Effects of Ezetimibe Combination Therapy for Patients With Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: Randomized Comparison of LDL Cholesterol Targeting <70 versus <55 mg/dL) conducted at 17 centers in South Korea, a total of 3048 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were enrolled between January 2021 and July 2022. Following the first randomization to either an intensive (<55 mg/dL) or conventional (<70 mg/dL) LDL-C–targeting strategy, patients underwent subsequent randomization (initial statin–ezetimibe combination therapy [n=1525] versus statin monotherapy [n=1523]) and were followed up for 3 years. Lipid-lowering therapy was adjusted according to a predefined protocol to achieve LDL-C targets. The primary end point was a 3-year composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, any revascularization, or hospitalization for unstable angina. The mean±SD age was 64.4±9.0 years, and 638 patients (20.9%) were female. The incidence of the primary end point did not differ between statin–ezetimibe combination therapy (128 patients [8.5%]) and statin monotherapy (119 patients [7.9%]; hazard ratio, 1.07 [95% CI, 0.83–1.37]; P =0.596). Patients who received statin–ezetimibe combination therapy achieved lower median LDL-C levels during follow-up than those who received statin monotherapy in both the intensive-targeting (53 mg/dL [interquartile range, 45–62 mg/dL] versus 62 mg/dL [interquartile range, 53–74 mg/dL]) and conventional-targeting (63 mg/dL [interquartile range, 55–73 mg/dL] versus 70 mg/dL [interquartile range, 62–81 mg/dL]) strategies. During follow-up, ezetimibe was added to the treatment regimen of 241 patients (34.3%) and 177 patients (24.8%) who initially received statin monotherapy in the intensive- and conventional-targeting strategies, respectively. The treatment effect of intensive-targeting versus conventional-targeting strategies was consistent regardless of therapy regimens without significant heterogeneity ( P interaction =0.583). The safety end points were similar between the groups. Within a target-directed LDL-C–lowering strategy, cardiovascular efficacy and safety did not differ significantly, whether initiated as statin–ezetimibe combination therapy or as statin monotherapy, but combination therapy facilitated achievement of a lower LDL-C target. n60d37fd229c3: To our knowledge, this is the first randomised trial to compare P2Y12 inhibitor strategies specifically in patients with AMI-CS. Cangrelor achieved effective platelet inhibition more frequently than crushed ticagrelor at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Non-inferiority of cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor was not demonstrated for the primary 30-day clinical endpoint. These trial findings can inform future trials of P2Y12 inhibition strategies in patients with AMI-CS.
n80eebaeebd9f: Background: Donation after circulatory death (DCD) heart transplantation has expanded rapidly, but outcomes across a broad range of donor ages remain unclear. Early DCD programs limited donor age to under 40 years over concerns that warm ischemia could worsen age-related cardiovascular changes. We hypothesized that DCD heart transplantation is associated with comparable outcomes to donation after brain death (DBD) through five years, without significant effect modification by donor age. Methods: Adult isolated primary heart transplants from 2019 through 2025 were analyzed using the United Network for Organ Sharing registry. Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional-hazards models, stratified by transplant year, compared DCD and DBD recipients. Models adjusted for recipient age, sex, body mass index (BMI), creatinine, and bilirubin, as well as donor sex and BMI. Donor age was evaluated as a continuous effect modifier. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality at one and five years. Secondary outcomes included graft failure, stroke, dialysis, permanent pacemaker implantation, and treated rejection within one year. Results: Among 21,970 recipients with available follow-up, 2,698 (12.3%) received DCD hearts. DCD use rose from 0.3% in 2019 to 25.3% in 2025. One-year mortality was similar between groups (unadjusted HR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.79-1.08; P=0.324). In the adjusted model, DCD was not associated with increased one-year mortality at donor age 40 (HR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.68-1.03; P=0.101), and donor age did not modify this association (P-interaction=0.131). One-year graft failure was also similar at donor age 40 (HR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.70-1.05; P=0.138; P-interaction=0.219). At five years, mortality remained comparable (unadjusted HR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.87-1.13; P=0.919). DCD was not associated with increased adjusted five-year mortality at donor age 40 (HR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.72-1.02; P=0.077); however, the relative DCD-versus-DBD hazard became more favorable with increasing donor age (interaction HR per 10 years, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75-0.99; P-interaction=0.037). Post-transplant dialysis was more frequent after DCD (20.4% vs 16.0%; P<0.001). Stroke, pacemaker implantation, and treated rejection did not differ between groups. Conclusions: In this national registry analysis, DCD heart transplantation was associated with similar one-year and five-year survival compared with DBD. Although donor age did not modify one-year outcomes, increasing donor age was associated with a more favorable relative hazard for DCD at five years. These findings support continued evaluation of donor-age thresholds for DCD heart use. The higher rate of post-transplant dialysis warrants further investigation.
nfbb4e9a1be21: Background: Where a person lives shapes cardiometabolic risk, yet the biological intermediates are poorly defined. Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT), a metabolically active visceral depot surrounding the coronary arteries, is a candidate intermediate: its volume and computed tomography (CT) attenuation track adiposity and cardiovascular risk. We hypothesized that greater neighborhood disadvantage is associated with larger EAT volume and lower CT attenuation, reflecting differences in both epicardial fat quantity and composition. Methods: We studied 26,826 adults undergoing coronary artery calcium CT in the Houston Methodist HeartScan Registry, with EAT volume and mean attenuation quantified automatically from CT images using a validated deep-learning model (DeepFat 2.0; fat window –190 to –30 HU). Residential addresses were geocoded to census tract and linked to the Area Deprivation Index (ADI), a Climate Vulnerability Index (CVI), and the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI). Each index was modeled in quartiles (Q4 vs Q1) and per standard deviation (SD) by linear regression, with tests for trend. Models were sequential: unadjusted; adjusted for age, sex, and race/ethnicity (primary); and further adjusted for cardiometabolic factors (body mass index [BMI], type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and smoking) to assess partial mediation by cardiometabolic factors. Results: All three indices showed graded associations with EAT volume and mean attenuation (all p<0.001). In the primary demographic model, the most- versus least-disadvantaged quartile was associated with greater EAT volume: +18.2 cm 3 for ADI, +12.8 cm 3 for CVI, and +3.2 cm 3 for SVI, as well as lower mean attenuation: –2.2 HU for ADI, –2.0 HU for CVI, and –0.5 HU for SVI . Continuous analyses were concordant, with each SD higher index associated with greater EAT volume (+6.6, +4.9, and +1.4 cm 3 per SD for ADI, CVI, and SVI, respectively). After further adjustment for cardiometabolic factors, volume associations attenuated but persisted for ADI and CVI (+7.3 and +5.6 cm 3 ; both p<0.001) and were no longer significant for SVI, suggesting that measured cardiometabolic factors accounted for part of these associations. In contrast, the attenuation shift remained for all three indices after cardiometabolic adjustment (–1.6, –1.5, and –0.4 HU). Conclusions: In a large CT registry, greater neighborhood disadvantage across three validated indices was associated with larger epicardial fat volume and lower attenuation. The volume association was diminished after adjustment for cardiometabolic factors, whereas the attenuation shift persisted, suggesting place-based disadvantage relates to both the quantity and composition of epicardial fat. EAT may represent an imaging intermediate linking environmental disadvantage to cardiometabolic disease and a potential target for prevention.
n42d6f55a4011: Background: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) face substantial in-hospital mortality following acute myocardial infarction (AMI). While glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) reduce long-term major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), their association with in-hospital outcomes during AMI remains incompletely defined in contemporary national datasets. Methods: We analyzed the 2023 National Inpatient Sample, the first dataset capturing a full calendar year of GLP-1 RA use (ICD-10-CM Z79.85). Adult T2DM hospitalizations with atherothrombotic AMI were included, excluding type 1 diabetes and demand ischemia. Patients with antecedent GLP-1 RA use (n=2,058) were matched 1:1 to controls using doubly robust propensity score methods, yielding 4,116 hospitalizations (20,580 weighted encounters) adjusted for 24 clinical and socioeconomic covariates, including comorbidity burden and hospital characteristics (Figure 1). The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, MACE, respiratory failure, sepsis, and resource utilization. Results: Post-matching balance was excellent (mean standardized mean difference 1.6%). GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower mortality (2.5% vs 5.1%; aOR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38-0.79; p=0.001). GLP-1 RA users also had lower odds of MACE-4 (aOR 0.57; p<0.001), cardiogenic shock (aOR 0.63; p=0.002), ischemic stroke (aOR 0.46; p=0.001), and cardiac arrest (aOR 0.71; p=0.046) (Figure 2). Non-cardiac complications, including respiratory failure (aOR 0.68; p<0.001) and sepsis (aOR 0.61; p=0.001), were also less frequent, while acute kidney injury was similar (aOR 0.94; p=0.470). GLP-1 RA users had shorter length of stay (4.27 vs 5.09 days; p<0.001) and lower hospital charges (p=0.019). Findings were directionally consistent across eight pre-specified clinical subgroups. A comprehensive summary of study design, outcomes, and interpretation is shown in Figure 3. Conclusions: Among hospitalized patients with T2DM and AMI, antecedent GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower odds of in-hospital mortality, cardiovascular events, and selected non-cardiac complications. These associations should be interpreted cautiously given the observational design and potential for residual confounding and healthy user effects, as patients receiving GLP-1 RAs may differ in access to care, treatment adherence, and baseline health status. The consistency and magnitude of these associations across outcomes and subgroups support the need for prospective studies to better define the relationship between GLP-1 RA therapy and acute cardiovascular outcomes.
n3887755443d8: Background: Cardiac myosin inhibitors (CMIs), mavacamten and aficamten, directly regulate sarcomeric hypercontractility in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). However, their comparative effectiveness, phenotype-specific effects, and safety profiles are inconsistently reported. Objectives: To assess the efficacy and safety of CMIs and analyze predefined subgroups based on drug (mavacamten vs. aficamten) and phenotype (obstructive vs. non-obstructive HCM). Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to September 19, 2025. Data were pooled using random-effects models for continuous and binary outcomes, and certainty was graded using GRADE. Eight RCTs enrolling 1,581 participants were included. Results: CMIs significantly improved the primary efficacy outcomes: peak VO 2 (MD 1.25 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 0.43-2.07) and reduced both resting LVOT gradient (MD -57.27 mmHg [-63.05 to -51.49]) and post-Valsalva LVOT gradient (MD -53.00 mmHg [-61.99 to -44.01]), with benefits predominantly in obstructive HCM. For secondary outcomes, CMIs improved symptoms (KCCQ-CSS: MD 6.42 [3.99-8.86]; NYHA improvement: OR 2.50 [2.03-3.09]) and reduced NT-proBNP and troponin I levels, albeit with inter-study variability. Aficamten produced greater gains in peak VO 2 and NYHA class, whereas mavacamten showed stronger gradient reduction; subgroup differences were not definitive. Adverse events were slightly more frequent with CMIs (OR 1.35, p = 0.02), mainly with mavacamten, but serious events were not increased (RR 1.09, p = 0.55). Conclusions: CMIs significantly enhance hemodynamic and symptomatic outcomes, with maximal benefit in obstructive HCM and an acceptable safety profile. Comparative and long-term trials are warranted. Keywords: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; cardiac myosin inhibitors; mavacamten; aficamten; LVOT gradient; peak VO 2 ; KCCQ; NYHA; NT-proBNP; troponin I.
nc2ebc39c524d: Background: Orforglipron, an oral non-peptide glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, is being evaluated for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity, both major contributors to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. However, a comprehensive quantitative synthesis of its efficacy and safety across doses and patient phenotypes is lacking. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of orforglipron versus placebo in adults with T2DM and/or obesity, perform prespecified subgroup analyses by dose and metabolic phenotype, and assess evidence certainty using GRADE and trial sequential analysis (TSA). Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, randomized controlled trials comparing orforglipron with placebo were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis to estimate mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity (I 2 ), leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, dose groups (3, 6, 24, 36 mg), and phenotype subgroups (obese/non-diabetic vs non-obese/diabetic) were evaluated; TSA assessed required information size and monitoring boundaries. Results: Five trials (n=2,672; orforglipron 1,413; placebo 1,259) were included. Orforglipron reduced HbA1c (primary MD –1.07%, 95% CI –2.00 to –0.13; I 2 =100%; sensitivity MD –1.45%, 95% CI –1.49 to –1.41; I 2 =0%), body weight (primary MD –5.25 kg, 95% CI –6.72 to –3.77; I 2 =96%; sensitivity MD –4.21 kg, 95% CI –4.40 to –4.02; I 2 =0%), BMI (MD –1.99 kg/m 2 , 95% CI –2.97 to –1.01; I 2 =97%), and systolic blood pressure (primary MD –3.90 mmHg, 95% CI –6.44 to –1.35; I 2 =91%; sensitivity MD –2.56 mmHg, 95% CI –4.64 to –0.48; I 2 =22%). Fasting plasma glucose also decreased significantly (MD –25.77 mg/dL, 95% CI –58.70 to –7.18), with evidence of a dose-response relationship. Diastolic blood pressure remained neutral (primary MD –0.32 mmHg, 95% CI –2.36 to 1.71; sensitivity MD +0.68 mmHg, 95% CI –0.02 to 1.39), while heart rate increased (primary MD +6.38 bpm, 95% CI +2.99 to +9.77). Hypoglycemia (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.23-4.86) and serious adverse events (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.75-1.62) were similar to placebo. TSA supported robust evidence for weight, BMI, and SBP, whereas additional data are needed for DBP, heart rate, hypoglycemia, and serious adverse events. Conclusions: Orforglipron significantly improves glycaemic control and cardiometabolic parameters, including HbA1c, body weight, BMI, SBP, and fasting plasma glucose. A class-consistent increase in heart rate was observed without increased hypoglycaemia or serious adverse events. Sensitivity analyses reduced heterogeneity while preserving effect estimates. TSA suggests robust evidence for weight, BMI, and SBP, but longer-term comparative trials are needed to clarify effects on DBP and safety outcomes. Keywords: Orforglipron; GLP-1 receptor agonist; type 2 diabetes; obesity; meta-analysis; GRADE; trial sequential analysis; HbA1c; blood pressure; heart rate.
nd2fbe6c90fb9: Introduction/Background: Left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP) has emerged as an alternative to biventricular pacing (BVP) for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT). Despite established benefits of BVP-CRT, approximately 30-40% of patients remain non-responders due to suboptimal coronary sinus lead positioning, unfavorable venous anatomy, or phrenic nerve stimulation. LBBAP engages the native conduction system to achieve more physiological activation. However, comparative effectiveness across hard clinical endpoints remains uncertain, and prior meta-analyses included fewer than 10 studies without randomized data. Hypothesis: LBBAP is superior to BVP for CRT across clinical, echocardiographic, and procedural safety outcomes. Methods: A systematic review following PRISMA guidelines was conducted across PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov through January 2025. Inclusion criteria were comparative studies of LBBAP versus BVP in CRT-indicated patients. Random-effects meta-analysis (DerSimonian-Laird) was performed. Primary outcome was the composite of all-cause death or heart failure hospitalization (HFH). Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, HFH, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) improvement, paced QRS duration, echocardiographic response, and procedural complications. Heterogeneity was quantified using Cochran Q and I-squared. Results: Twenty-one studies (3 randomized controlled trials, 18 observational; 5,812 patients; follow-up 6-37 months) were included. LBBAP significantly reduced the composite endpoint (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.49-0.73, P<0.00001; 10 studies; I-squared=53.5%), all-cause mortality (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.70-0.90, P=0.0003; 9 studies; I-squared=0%), and HFH (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.49-0.65, P<0.00001; 8 studies; I-squared=0%). LBBAP achieved greater LVEF improvement (MD +3.96%, 95% CI 3.02-4.90, P<0.00001; 15 studies; I-squared=18.7%), narrower paced QRS (MD -17.5ms, 95% CI -19.6 to -15.3, P<0.00001; 15 studies; I-squared=38.2%), higher echocardiographic response (OR 2.54, 95% CI 1.87-3.46, P<0.00001; 16 studies; I-squared=66.0%), and fewer procedural complications (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.34-0.63, P<0.00001; 8 studies; I-squared=0%). Subgroup analysis confirmed consistent benefits in RCTs (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21-0.80) and observational studies (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.52-0.77). Conclusions: In this comprehensive meta-analysis of 21 studies including 3 RCTs and 5,812 patients, LBBAP demonstrated superiority over BVP across all seven assessed endpoints. LBBAP reduced death or HFH by 40%, all-cause mortality by 20%, and HFH by 44%, while achieving superior reverse remodeling, electrical resynchronization, and procedural safety. These findings support LBBAP as a preferred first-line CRT strategy.
nd1ec5cf229d1: Background: Left ventricular end-diastolic dimension (LVEDD) is a key echocardiographic marker of adverse remodeling in heart failure (HF). While guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) can attenuate LV dilation, pacing modality, particularly the physiologic resynchronization achieved by left bundle branch pacing (LBBP), has garnered increasing interest. Patients with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (NICM), who are more likely to respond favorably to resynchronization, remain a critical population for evaluation. Objective: To assess the impact of LBBP versus biventricular pacing (BiV) on LVEDD in a NICM-enriched, GDMT-treated CRT population. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted per PRISMA guidelines. Thirteen studies comparing LBBP and BiV were identified; nine reporting end-study LVEDD were included. Subgroup analyses were performed by baseline LVEF (<30% vs ≥30%), follow-up duration (<12 vs ≥12 months), and GDMT optimization (if ≥80% of LBBP patients received at least 3 of the pillars). For studies without stratified LVEF data, subgroup classification was estimated conservatively using mean±SD. Mean differences (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using a fixed-effects model. Across studies, 78% of patients had NICM, and >85% received GDMT (BB, ACEi/ARB, MRA). Results: LBBP significantly reduced LVEDD compared to BiV (MD -4.15 mm [-5.96, -2.35]; P <0.0001). In patients with ≥12 months follow-up (n=5), the effect was more pronounced (MD -5.96 mm [-8.13, -3.79]; I2=0%), while no significant effect was observed in studies with <12 months (MD -0.16 mm [-3.39, 3.07]; I2=90%). The subgroup interaction by follow-up duration was significant (P =0.004), supporting a time-dependent remodeling effect. LBBP also reduced LVEDD in both optimized GDMT (MD -3.80 mm [-5.69, -1.92]; I2=83%) and non-optimized groups (MD -7.73 mm [-13.78, -1.68]; I2=0%), with no significant interaction (P =0.23), suggesting that the remodeling benefit of LBBP is consistent and additive across varying levels of pharmacologic optimization. Conclusion: In a predominantly NICM, GDMT-treated CRT population, LBBP was associated with a greater reduction in LVEDD than BiV pacing. The benefit was consistent across LVEF and GDMT subgroups and more evident with longer follow-up, supporting a progressive and physiologic reverse remodeling effect of LBBP beyond what is achievable with GDMT alone.
n6be65b6b2034: Introduction/Background: Right heart catheterization metrics are preload and afterload-dependent, masking underlying ventricular function. Single-beat estimation of the right ventricular (RV) pressure-volume loop yields load-independent metrics of intrinsic right ventricular (RV)-pulmonary vascular function that help guide care. These parameters are difficult to obtain, but we have developed a novel computational program that can extract these from the standard RV tracing image (Moon et al JACC HF 2026). We tested whether our program-derived RV end-systolic elastance (Ees), effective arterial elastance (Ea), and other pressure-volume loop metrics can predict poor outcomes in an Impella (Abiomed, MA) supported shock cohort. Methods: We retrospectively studied Impella-supported cardiogenic shock patients with baseline and subsequent hemodynamic data (n=55). Hemodynamic variables were collected at time 0 and 48 hours post-Impella implant (time 2d). RV waveforms collected at time 0 were inputted into the program alongside stroke volume to derive Ees, Ea, their ratio, as well as end-systolic volume (ESV), end-diastolic volume, and RV pressure-volume loops. Kruskal-Wallis and post-hoc testing compared program and hemodynamic metrics across three outcome groups: successful bridging to recovery or definitive surgery, need for MCS escalation, and death. We then investigated predictors of death. Results: Seven of the 55 patients died before successful bridging or MCS escalation. Outcomes were dichotomized into survivable (recovery or MCS escalation) and fatal (death). Pulmonary artery pulsatility index (log transformed PAPI), Ees, and ESV were significantly predictive of death (p<0.05). Change in RV cardiac power output (RV-CPO) from time 0 to time 2d was as well (p<0.05). The death group had the lowest change in RV-CPO (-0.02 ± 0.02 vs 0.06 ± 0.02) and lower logPAPI (0.29 ± 0.15 vs 0.89 ± 0.1), low Ees (0.32 ± 0.03 vs 0.59 ± 0.07), and elevated ESV (142.5 ±19.6 vs 91.6 ± 7.6) (Figure 1). Conclusion: Single beat-derived RV metrics, including Ees and ESV, helped supplement traditional metrics to predict death in an Impella-supported shock cohort. Low RV performance metrics and elevated RV ESV in those who died suggest that mortality may stem from biventricular failure not fully supported by univentricular mechanical support. Our program may add value to up front prognostication of shock patients undergoing Impella placement.
n8b7ea2e6a426: Introduction: While Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) improve outcomes in obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), their safety and efficacy in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) has not been established. The increased cyclic AMP signaling effect of GLP-1RA is a possible safety concern in patients with HFrEF, with prior trials suggesting potential increased risk for HF hospitalization (HFH). Given the closer biological alignment of HFmrEF with HFrEF than HFpEF, evaluating the safety of GLP-1RAs in this group is critical. Research Questions: Among patients with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and overtly symptomatic HFmrEF, are GLP-1RA associated with differences in HFH or all-cause mortality? Methods: PRAISE-HFmrEF is a nationwide multicenter cohort study across 170 US Veterans Affairs hospitals. Using centralized electronic health records (2000-2022), we identified patients with type 2 diabetes, obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m 2 ), and HFmrEF (LVEF 40-49%) using a validated algorithm. Patients were required to have loop diuretic prescriptions or elevated natriuretic peptides ( Figure 1 ). Using a target trial emulation framework with an active-comparator, new-user design, GLP-1RA initiators were compared to dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor or sulfonylurea (DPP4i/SU) initiators between 2015-2021. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) based on the propensity score balanced 31 covariates including demographics, comorbidities, HF severity indices, and baseline pharmacotherapy. The primary outcome was time to composite of HFH or all-cause mortality, assessed using doubly robust IPTW-Cox models. HFH was additionally evaluated using Fine-Grey competing risk models. Results: A total of 2,262 patients met the inclusion criteria (GLP-1RA: n=957; DPP4i/SU: n=1,305) ( Figure 1 ). Mean age was 68.7 ± 8.4 years, median BMI 36.6 kg/m 2 [IQR 33.5-41.4], 97.6% were male. After IPTW, all 31 covariates were well balanced (absolute standardized mean differences <10%) ( Figure 2 ). Over a median follow-up of 2.8 years, 1131 patients (50.5%) experienced the primary outcome. Crude incidence rates were 16.7 and 15.0 events per 100 person-years in the GLP-1RA and DPP4i/SU groups respectively. After adjustment, GLP-1RA was not associated with an increased risk of the primary outcome (IPTW HR 0.88, 95% CI: 0.73-1.05; p=0.16) ( Figure 3A ). Competing risk analysis showed no differences in HFH (subdistribution HR 1.00, 95% CI: 0.76-1.32). There was no heterogeneity across all tested subgroups ( Figure 3B ). Conclusions: In this nationwide cohort with obesity, diabetes, and rigorously phenotyped HFmrEF, GLP-1RA at diabetes management doses appear to be safe without evidence of adverse HF outcomes. However, the efficacy and safety at weight loses doses warrants further randomized evidence.
ne9e14ff8b7b9: Background: Patients with advanced liver disease often have elevated pulmonary artery pressures due to hyperdynamic circulation rather than true pulmonary vascular disease. Differentiating flow-mediated pulmonary hypertension from porto-pulmonary hypertension (PoPH) remains clinically challenging. Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) Doppler morphology reflects pulmonary vascular impedance and may improve noninvasive identification of elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). Research Question: Can RVOT Doppler morphology identify clinically significant pulmonary vascular disease in patients with advanced liver disease? Methods: We retrospectively studied 236 patients with advanced liver disease who underwent transthoracic echocardiography at Mayo Clinic between 2003 and 2023; 162 also underwent right heart catheterization. RVOT Doppler profiles were categorized as normal, early-peaking, notched with preserved late systolic flow, or notched with diminished late systolic flow. Diagnostic performance for elevated PVR (>2 and >3 Wood units [WU]) was evaluated. Results: RVOT Doppler morphology showed a strong, graded association with invasive pulmonary hemodynamics. Progressive abnormalities in RVOT flow patterns were associated with higher mean pulmonary artery pressure, higher pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), and lower cardiac output (all p<0.0001). Patients with normal and early peaking RVOT profiles had low PVR (1.2±0.6 and 1.3±0.8 WU, respectively), consistent with hyperdynamic physiology, whereas notched profiles identified patients with clinically significant pulmonary vascular disease. Abnormal RVOT morphology demonstrated excellent sensitivity for elevated PVR (98.2% for PVR >2 WU and 100% for PVR >3 WU), while RVOT mid-systolic notching showed high specificity (100% for PVR>2 and 93.9% for PVR>3). Based on these findings, we propose a stepwise diagnostic algorithm. Conclusions: RVOT Doppler morphology provides a simple, noninvasive physiologic marker of pulmonary vascular resistance in advanced liver disease. A stepwise RVOT-based diagnostic framework offers high sensitivity for screening and high specificity for confirming pulmonary vascular disease, with important implications for transplant risk stratification and selection of patients for invasive hemodynamic evaluation, but needs to be evaluated in larger patient cohorts.
n59d1ca258cd7: Background: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) reduce sudden cardiac death; however, characterization of the device problems reported in association with patient deaths relies on passive surveillance. The spectrum and temporal pattern of these reports across manufacturers and device families have not been systematically described in recent years. We present one decade of analysis of ICD-related deaths. Methods: We queried the FDA Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database for ICD device-related reports with a death outcome. From 7,065 records, we removed duplicates (n=150) and reports with no identified device problem or indeterminate classification, and restricted the dataset to event years 2016 onward, yielding 2,372 reports. Manufacturer labels were consolidated to parent companies; free-text device-problem codes were mapped to mechanistic families and to product families. Proportions are reported with 95% Wilson score confidence intervals. Results: Reports involved Medtronic (50.9%; 95% CI 48.8-53.0), Abbott/St. Jude (28.6%; 26.7-30.5), Boston Scientific (15.4%; 14.0-17.0), and Biotronik (3.5%). Sensing problems were most common (33.8%; 31.9-35.8), followed by therapy delivery (28.4%; 26.6-30.3), lead/hardware (15.7%), and pacing/capture (10.6%). The device-problem profile differed markedly by product family: Sprint Quattro reports were predominantly sensing-related (62.4%; 58.5-66.1), whereas Quadra/Unify Assura (59.2%) and Cobalt (62.2%) were dominated by therapy-delivery problems, and Endotak Reliance by lead/hardware (48.7%). Annual report volume was non-monotonic, falling from 264 (2016) to 168 (2019) before rising to 238 (2025). Conclusions: Sensing and therapy-delivery problems dominate ICD-related death reports, with distinct problem signatures across device families. While these unverified data cannot establish device safety or causation, characterizing reports by mechanism and product family highlights specific signals warranting verified investigation
n6a75d9ce1b6f: Background: Coronary artery-to-pulmonary artery fistula (CPAF) is an uncommon congenital coronary anomaly characterized by an abnormal communication between a coronary artery and the pulmonary artery, accounting for approximately 15%-30% of coronary artery fistulas. Although larger fistulas may cause myocardial ischemia, heart failure, arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, or coronary steal phenomenon, the clinical significance of many CPAFs remains uncertain. We present a complex case of CPAF in a patient with ventricular tachycardia, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, pulmonary hypertension, and concurrent substance abuse, highlighting the challenges of determining the clinical significance of an incidental coronary anomaly. Case Presentation: A 40-year-old man with a history of alcohol and cocaine abuse presented with palpitations and chest pain following recent cocaine use. On presentation, heart rate was 180-200 bpm and blood pressure was 89/78 mmHg. Electrocardiography demonstrated sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. The patient underwent successful synchronized cardioversion and was initiated on intravenous amiodarone. Repeat electrocardiography demonstrated normal sinus rhythm.Transthoracic echocardiography revealed newly reduced left ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 30%-34%. To evaluate for an ischemic etiology, coronary angiography was performed and demonstrated angiographically normal coronary arteries with a large communication between the left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) and the pulmonary artery. Coronary computed tomography angiography further characterized the anomaly as an 8-mm fistulous vessel originating from the proximal LAD and draining into the main pulmonary artery. Right heart catheterization demonstrated a non-significant shunt (Qp/Qs 0.81) and moderate-to-severe pulmonary hypertension. Given the absence of a hemodynamically significant shunt and the presence of alternative causes of the patient's cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia, including cocaine and alcohol use, invasive closure was deferred. The patient was discharged on amiodarone, guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure, and a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator. At three-month follow-up, repeat echocardiography demonstrated improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction to 35%-40%. Conclusion: This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of determining the clinical significance of CPAF in patients with multiple competing etiologies for ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmia. In the absence of a significant shunt or clear evidence of coronary steal, conservative management with optimization of medical therapy and risk-factor modification may be appropriate. Ongoing follow-up is warranted to reassess the need for intervention if symptoms or ventricular function fail to improve
nbedd466dd157: BACKGROUND: Infants born with hypoplastic left heart syndrome remain at high risk during the interstage between Stage 1 and Stage 2 surgical palliations. NPC-QIC previously reported an increase in interstage survival for these infants among participating centers through its Learning Health Network structure and methodology. We sought to evaluate whether this improvement was sustained over time. METHODS: Patients enrolled in the NPC-QIC registry who underwent Stage 1 surgical palliation and were discharged home during the interstage period were included. Patient characteristics in Phase 1 (2008-2016) and Phase 2 (2016-2026) were compared and rates of interstage survival, major adverse event readmissions, and growth failure were analyzed. RESULTS: A total of 5495 patients (Phase 1 – 2199, Phase 2 - 3296) were enrolled from 77 centers. Improvement in interstage survival noted in Phase 1 was sustained throughout Phase 2 at 94.8%. Major adverse event readmissions declined early in Phase 2 and were maintained (0.9 versus 1.74/100 interstage patients). Sustained reduction in growth failure remained stable over time. Phase 2 cohort had higher prevalence of RV-PA conduit, lower NEONATE score, higher digoxin prescription at Stage 1 discharge, and longer Stage 1 length of stay compared to Phase 1. CONCLUSIONS: Significant improvements in survival in the NPC-QIC interstage cohorts were sustained for 12 years. Major event readmissions declined and remained lower for 8 years, and adequate growth was sustained. The sustained improvement achieved by the 77 participating centers reflects continued adherence to improvement processes, collaborative learning, and promoting best practices over time, including utilization of digoxin and NEONATE score.
n564cd27750d3: Introduction: Neighborhood deprivation is an established risk factor for adverse cardiovascular outcomes, prompting the integration of the Social Deprivation Index (SDI) into clinical risk tools such as the AHA PREVENT equation. Although various neighborhood indices predict cardiovascular risk, their relative predictive power and the biological mechanisms linking deprivation to adverse events remain unknown. We hypothesized that the Area Deprivation Index (ADI), which captures neighborhood factors at the finer census block-group level, would outperform the tract-level Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and ZIP code-level (SDI) indices, and that chronic inflammation, indexed by the emerging immune biomarker suPAR, and the acute-phase reactant, hs-CRP, would mediate this association. Methods: Three commonly used indices were compared: ADI (national percentile 1-100, census block-group—the smallest census geographic unit), SVI (composite index 0-1, census tract), and SDI (percentile 1-100, ZIP code). Among 6,195 participants (mean age 62, 64% male, 24% Black) in the Emory Cardiovascular Biobank, a prospective cohort undergoing cardiac catheterization for suspected CAD, each index was evaluated for independent association with 4-point MACE (cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, or HF hospitalization) using multiply-imputed Cox models adjusted for demographics, cardiometabolic risk factors, and guideline-directed medications. Causal mediation analysis quantified the direct and inflammation-mediated impact of ADI on adverse events via suPAR and hs-CRP in the biomarker subcohort (n=3,841). Results: Over a median follow-up of 5.2 years, 1,682 participants (27%) experienced MACE. In fully adjusted analyses, residents who resided in the most disadvantaged neighborhoods had 33% higher risk of MACE than those in the least disadvantaged (ADI HR 1.33; 95% CI 1.15-1.53), with a graded dose-response (+13%, +20%, +33% across quartiles). SVI (HR 1.09; 0.94-1.26) and SDI (HR 1.07; 0.94-1.23) were not significant (Figure 1A-C). Systemic inflammation mediated ~40% (95% CI 27-69%) of ADI's effect on MACE; individually but not additively, suPAR and hs-CRP contributed 34% and 14%, respectively (Figure 1D). Conclusions: In a head-to-head comparison, only ADI, but neither SVI nor the AHA PREVENT calculator's ZIP code-derived SDI was independently associated with adverse cardiovascular events in individuals with CAD. Inflammation accounted for ~40% of the ADI-MACE association. ADI as an index of neighborhood health may be a useful tool for evaluating residual risk in patients with CAD. Whether anti-inflammatory interventions-pharmacologic and community-level, including access to safe, walkable neighborhoods, improved air quality, and healthier dietary patterns-can reduce neighborhood-mediated risk needs further evaluation.
n9b8f7a0b441e: BACKGROUND: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) for coronary artery disease (CAD) are heritable, with UK Biobank analyses demonstrating intra-familial correlations of r = 0.5 among first-degree relative pairs. Despite this promising data, prospective feasibility and yield of CAD-PRS cascade testing in preventive cardiology remain undefined. CASCADE-PRS is a prospective observational cohort study enrolling individuals with premature clinical or subclinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and their first-degree relatives at Penn Medicine, with the primary objective of characterizing intra-familial CAD-PRS correlation. MethodS: Probands were eligible if they had premature clinical ASCVD (CAD, peripheral artery disease [PAD], large-artery ischemic stroke prior to age 55 (males) or 65 (females), subclinical ASCVD (carotid intima media thickness [CIMT] or coronary artery calcification score [CACS] >75th percentile for age). Known monogenic lipid disorders were excluded. CAD-PRS testing was performed via buccal swab by Allelica Multi-Ancestry CAD-PRS Test. High-risk PRS was defined per individualized Allelica thresholds (≥2-fold relative risk). This interim analysis describes enrollment status, baseline demographics, and prevalence of high-risk CAD-PRS. ResultS: As of May 2026, 20 probands and 26 family members (at least one per proband) had been enrolled (of a total of 59 individuals contacted) and PRS results were available for 15 probands and at least one relative (n=17). Probands were older (63.4 ± 9.5 vs. 42.1 ± 16.7 years), more likely to be male (73% vs. 41%), and predominantly White (87% probands, 82% relatives). Mean PRS percentile was similar between probands and relatives (55.7 ± 27.3 vs. 55.5 ± 27.8). High-risk PRS was identified in 3 of 15 probands (20%) and 2 of 17 relatives (12%). Among relatives of high-risk probands, 2 of 3 met the high-risk threshold (vs 0/14 relatives of non-high-risk probands); the third relative of a high risk proband had a PRS at the 82 nd percentile, just below the individualized high-risk threshold of 83 — overall suggesting intra-familial concordance. ConclusionS: To our knowledge, CASCADE-PRS is the first prospective study of intra-familial CAD-PRS concordance in a preventive cardiology setting. The 78% consent rate demonstrates robust clinical feasibility and patient engagement. High-risk PRS was identified in 20% of probands and was enriched among their first-degree relatives (67% vs 0% of relatives of non-high-risk probands), demonstrating early familial clustering. This strategy identifies high genetic risk individuals, which is particularly useful in younger adults. Continued enrollment will enable formal assessment of intra-familial PRS correlation and downstream clinical impact.
n34bf06fd1a7c: Purpose: We aimed to evaluate the clinical feasibility of combining coronary sinus flow reserve measurement and non-contrast stress T1 mapping via simultaneous hybrid PET/MR imaging to predict impaired global myocardial flow reserve in patients with ischemic heart disease. Methods: Consecutive 104 patients (mean age: 66 ± 14 years; 87 males) who underwent rest-adenosine stress 13 N-ammonia PET/MR were retrospectively enrolled. Coronary sinus flow reserve (CSFr) was calculated from rest and stress coronary sinus flow measurements obtained using phase-contrast cine CMR. Non-contrast T1 mapping was performed using the MOLLI sequence, and T1 reactivity was calculated as the percentage change from rest to stress. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were conducted for T1 reactivity and CSFr individually. Subsequently, a multi-parametric logistic regression model was constructed by combining both parameters to generate a joint ROC curve based on the derived predictive probabilities. Myocardial flow reserve (MFR) obtained via rest-stress PET served as the reference standard, and impaired MFR was defined as MFR < 2.0. Results: In the univariate ROC analysis, both parameters demonstrated significant predictive values for impaired MFR; CSF showed an AUC of 0.75 (95% CI: 0.64-0.87, p = 0.0003), and T1 reactivity showed an AUC of 0.66 (95% CI: 0.54-0.78, p = 0.0066). The combined model integrating both CSFr and T1 reactivity demonstrated an improved diagnostic accuracy, yielding an AUC of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.74-0.93, p < 0.0001). At the optimal combined predictive score cut-off of 0.74, the joint model provided a sensitivity of 87.1% and a specificity of 73.7%. Conclusion: The combination of CSFr and T1 reactivity improves the prediction of impaired MFR. This multi-parametric CMR approach may serve as a radiation-free, and non-contrast tool for evaluating coronary vasodilatory capacity during routine stress CMR.
nd2f99d7273e5: Background: Cardiac surgery induces systemic inflammation that may promote persistent monocyte reprogramming. While prior studies have focused on postoperative phenotypic recovery, DNA methylation profiling may better define monocyte diversification and its regulatory mechanisms. We hypothesized that perioperative stress promotes persistent diversification of monocyte phenotypes that can be identified through DNA methylation profiling. Methods: Blood samples were obtained from patients undergoing non-emergent cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (n = 40) at baseline, 7 days, and 3 months after surgery. Monocytes were isolated by negative selection and analyzed by genome-wide DNA methylation profiling (Illumina MethylationEPIC array) and RNA sequencing. Methylation and transcriptomic profiles were compared with curated reference datasets representing distinct monocyte activation states. Resolution of systemic inflammation was assessed by serum interleukin-6(IL-6). Results: Serum IL-6 levels normalized by postoperative day 7, indicating resolution of systemic inflammation. In contrast, postoperative changes in the monocyte methylation landscape were more diverse than changes in transcriptomic activity and persisted through 3 months. Relative CpG enrichment analysis demonstrated that perioperative monocytes acquired features consistent with neuroinflammatory, tumor-associated, and pathogen-defense phenotypes, whereas atherosclerotic and foam cell-like signatures were less prominent. Temporal analysis of differentially methylated sites revealed regulatory features consistent with activated and metabolically stressed immune cells adapting to inflammation, hypoxia, and endoplasmic reticulum stress. Overlap between transcriptomic and methylation profiles suggested coordinated regulation of pathways involved in negative immune activation and NF-κB-associated signaling. Conclusion: Cardiac surgery induce epigenetic diversification of circulating monocytes, even after apparent resolution of systemic inflammation during postoperative recovery. These findings suggest that CpG methylation profiling may reveal persistent postoperative monocyte reprogramming not fully captured by transcriptomic or conventional inflammatory markers.
n8de51c852640: Background: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) reflects cumulative coronary atherosclerotic burden and is a strong predictor of cardiovascular events. Obesity is also associated with increased cardiometabolic risk. It remains unclear whether body mass index (BMI) alters the prognostic performance of CAC or whether the contribution of BMI to cardiovascular risk varies across levels of atherosclerotic burden. We evaluated whether the association between BMI and incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) varies according to CAC burden. Methods: We conducted a prospective cohort study of adults without known cardiovascular disease undergoing CAC screening within the CLARIFY multicenter registry. Participants were categorized by CAC burden (0, 1-99, 100-399, >= 400) and BMI category. The primary outcome was incident five-point MACE occurring more than six months after CAC assessment. Kaplan Meier methods were used to estimate cumulative event rates across CAC and BMI strata, with differences assessed using the log-rank test. Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, race, smoking status, LDL cholesterol, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and preventive medication use were used to estimate associations and test for CACхBMI interaction. Results: Among 178,525 participants (mean age 59 years; 53% female), 8,922 MACE events occurred over a median follow-up of 2.6 years. CAC was strongly associated with incident MACE across all BMI categories, with progressively higher event rates observed at increasing CAC levels (all p<0.001). Within CAC strata, the association between BMI and MACE varied according to CAC burden. Compared with normal BMI, class II-III obesity was associated with a 35-58% higher adjusted risk of MACE among individuals with CAC=0 (p<0.001). However, BMI-related differences in risk progressively diminished with increasing CAC burden and were no longer statistically significant among individuals with CAC>=400. At CAC>=400, adjusted MACE risk did not differ meaningfully by BMI category (overweight HR 1.05, class I obesity HR 1.08, class II obesity HR 1.10, class III obesity HR 1.12; all 95% CI crossed 1). A statistically significant but modest CACхBMI interaction was observed (p<0.001), indicating that the association between BMI and MACE was attenuated at higher CAC levels, whereas the association between CAC and MACE remained robust across BMI categories. Conclusions: CAC was a robust predictor of cardiovascular events across all BMI categories. In contrast, obesity related differences in cardiovascular risk were most evident among individuals with little or no coronary calcification and diminished with increasing CAC burden. These findings support the use of CAC for cardiovascular risk stratification regardless of BMI and suggest that increasing atherosclerotic burden diminishes the relative prognostic contribution of BMI.
n93d460ecd6c1: Background: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity disproportionately affecting socially marginalized populations. Whether county-level social vulnerability modifies the temporal trajectory of PAD mortality remains unknown. We examined 20-year trends in PAD mortality across the spectrum of social vulnerability in Florida counties. Methods: We extracted county-level age-adjusted PAD mortality rates (AAMR, per 100,000) from the CDC Wide-Ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (WONDER) database (ICD-10: I70-I78, 2000-2020) for 56 Florida counties with reliable data (≥20 deaths per period). Counties were linked to the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and categorized into five groups (Group I: SVI 0-0.2 [least vulnerable] to Group V: SVI 0.81-1.0 [most vulnerable]). We calculated relative percentage change in AAMR between 2000-2003 and 2016-2019 and used adjusted linear regression to evaluate the association between SVI group and temporal change in AAMR, adjusting for county-level prevalence of poverty, unemployment, lack of insurance, and educational attainment. Results: Overall PAD AAMR declined 46.1% across Florida (38.0 to 20.5 per 100,000, 2000-2003 to 2016-2019). Across all periods, AAMR was significantly higher in more vulnerable counties (Group I: 20.9 vs. Group V: 34.9 per 100,000; Kruskal-Wallis p<0.001). However, the most socially vulnerable counties (Group V) demonstrated the greatest absolute improvement, with a 61.2% decline in AAMR versus 51.2% in Group I. In unadjusted analysis, higher SVI was not significantly associated with differential improvement (β=1.38 per SVI quintile, p=0.35). After covariate adjustment, county-level unemployment independently attenuated PAD mortality improvement (β=–4.74, p=0.033), while the SVI association approached but did not reach significance (β=4.39, p=0.052). Conclusions: Despite persistently higher PAD mortality burden in socially vulnerable Florida counties, improvement over two decades was comparable or greater across all SVI groups — a pattern distinct from overall cardiovascular mortality trends. County-level unemployment emerged as a specific attenuating factor independent of global social vulnerability. These findings highlight the need for targeted vascular care interventions in high-unemployment communities and underscore the importance of condition-specific disparity analyses beyond composite cardiovascular outcomes.
ne628de89ead8: Background: Electrocardiogram (ECG) foundation models (FMs) have been shown to improve diagnostic performance compared to traditional ECG artificial intelligence (AI) methods. While FMs in other domains show performance benefits with pretraining data scaling, it is unclear whether similar relationships govern ECG FMs and if such relationships are consistent across demographic strata. Research Questions: We evaluate how pretraining data scaling affects ECG-AI performance across racial groups and the sexes for structural heart disease (SHD) tasks. Methods: We pretrained an ECG vision transformer (1D-ViT) using masked auto-encoding, by hiding 60% of the ECG and training the model to reconstruct the waveform. Pretraining scales from no pre-training to 800 thousand (k) ECGs were curated from the MIMIC-IV database. Fine-tuning and evaluation used the EchoNext database with 12 SHD tasks. All ECGs were normalized to the respective dataset’s mean and standard deviation and reduced to the 8 linearly independent leads: Lead I, Lead II, and V1-V6. Multi-label fine-tuning for each SHD label maximized area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). The top 4 transformer blocks and classification head were updated, while the remaining 8 transformer blocks were frozen. A control model had all layers trained without pre-training weights. All models used EchoNext's predefined train, validation, and test folds and were evaluated for AUROC. Aggregate performance across all labels was assessed for white, black, hispanic, male and female categories. We bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals with 2000 repetitions. Results: Aggregate performance peaked at the 800k scale with AUROCs of 0.825 (0.807-0.843) ,0.838 (0.814-0.859), 0.826 (0.799-0.849), 0.825 (0.806-0.843), and 0.840 (0.824-0.854) for White, Black, Hispanic, male, and female categories respectively. For all categories, smaller scales of 50k and 100k worsened performance compared to the control. Performance tended to approach the control at scales of 200k and 400k and surpassed the control by 600k. Conclusions: Across all demographic strata, the models showed similar behavior: smaller pretraining scales underperformed the control, while larger pretraining scales improved performance. This suggests a generalizable trend that ECG-AI pretraining benefits only emerge after a minimum scale threshold. Experiments across greater logarithmic orders are needed to assess the point of performance saturation.
n9bd3a07a37f3: Background: Ductal artery stenting (DAS) has emerged as a preferred palliative strategy instead of surgical shunts (BTTS) for neonates with ductal-dependent pulmonary blood flow (DDPBF). Previous studies in BTTS, as well as in other neonatal surgical cohorts, suggest worse outcomes in low birthweight (LBW) patients. Yet, there are no comparable data on mortality or other outcomes among LBW neonates undergoing DAS. We studied early outcomes for LBW neonates following successful DAS using contemporary data. Methods: Neonates in the Congenital Cardiac Research Collaborative (CCRC) DDPBF registry with index palliation occurring from 2021-2025 were included in this study. LBW was defined as <2.5kg, and also analyzed as a continuous variable. The primary outcome was death during the index hospitalization. Secondary outcomes included major life-threatening events (ECMO or emergent reintervention for life-threatening cyanosis), any reintervention for cyanosis, and complications from the index procedure. Results: There were 509 neonates from 16 centers who underwent DAS (birthweight range 1.4 - 4.3kg), of which 107 (21%) were <2.5 kg (LBW). LBW neonates were of younger gestational age (37 vs. 39 weeks, p<0.001), had more extracardiac anomalies (44% vs. 29%, p=0.004), and were more likely to be managed under a single-ventricle pathway (53% vs. 42%, p=0.008). LBW neonates underwent DAS at a later age compared to neonates ≥ 2.5kg (12 vs. 7 days of life, p<0.001), with similar distributions for percutaneous access site, number of stents, and pulmonary artery jailing. In total, there were 21 deaths (4.1%) during the initial hospitalization, 47 (9.2%) major life-threatening events, and 151 (30%) reinterventions for cyanosis, with no significant difference by birthweight. Procedural complications were more prevalent among LBW neonates (23 vs. 13%, p=0.014). Thrombus, vascular injury, and arrhythmia requiring therapy at initial palliation were the most common complications. LBW using 2.5 kg as a cut-point was not significantly associated with mortality (unadjusted OR= 1.94 95% CI 0.76 - 4.93; adjusted OR= 2.60 95% CI 0.99 - 6.84). However, in a multivariable model using birthweight as a continuous variable, larger birthweight was significantly associated with decreased risk for mortality (OR 0.37 95% CI 0.17 - 0.84, p= 0.018; Figure 1). Conclusion: In contrast to prior studies, overall early mortality in this cohort of DDPBF neonates undergoing DAS was low at 4.1%. While LBW was not associated with increased mortality risk using 2.5 kg as a cut-point, there was a significantly decreased risk with increasing birthweight when treated as a continuous variable. Procedural complications were also significantly higher for LBW neonates. Further investigation using this comprehensive registry will elucidate additional risk factors and optimize future outcomes for this vulnerable population.
neb88cf5b0161: Introduction: External iliac artery endofibrosis (EIAE) affects avid cyclists who undergo repetitive hip flexion during high endurance activity. Increased mechanical stress and blood flow lead to intimal thickening and non-atherosclerotic stenosis, resulting in exercise-induced claudication. Unlike atherosclerotic peripheral artery disease, EIAE occurs in otherwise healthy athletes and is frequently missed due to its resting-asymptomatic nature, making incidental discovery during vascular imaging an unusual diagnostic pathway. Case: A 52-year-old female with hyperlipidemia and lacunar infarcts presented with recent cryptogenic stroke. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with right-to-left shunting, and she underwent successful percutaneous closure. Post-procedural groin bleeding prompted abdominal aortogram with runoff to exclude dissection, fistula, and perforation. Incidentally, significant stenosis of the external iliac artery was identified. Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) revealed a minimal lumen area of 3.7 mm 2 , below the 4.0 mm 2 hemodynamic significant threshold, alongside the pathognomonic "perfect circle appearance" — circumferential intimal thickening with preserved outer wall architecture. This imaging finding is distinctly absent in atherosclerotic disease. Directed history confirmed she was a long-time avid cyclist. Discussion: Repetitive hip flexion causes arterial stretching, kinking, and elevated shear stress, driving smooth muscle proliferation and subintimal fibrosis without lipid deposition. Symptoms are classically exertional and rapidly resolve with rest, a pattern easily attributed to musculoskeletal etiology, underscoring the diagnostic challenge. Untreated, complications include thrombosis, dissection, and secondary atheroma. Management options include endarterectomy, endofibrosectomy, or endovascular stenting, selected based on lesion severity and patient activity demands. Conclusion: This case highlights the unique imaging features of EIAE, a peripheral vascular disease seen in athletes. IVUS is the modality of choice, demonstrating circumferential intimal thickening and constrictive remodeling in the absence of traditional atherosclerotic risk factors. Clinicians should maintain awareness of EIAE in physically active patients, as early recognition enables targeted intervention and return to full activity.
n319d4a490d5a: Introduction: Coronary artery aneurysms are uncommon and may be discovered during evaluation of chest pain. Their clinical significance depends not only on size and anatomy, but also on whether they impair myocardial perfusion. We report a rare case of a large left main (LM) coronary aneurysm causing inducible ischemia. Case: A 49-year-old woman with hyperlipidemia presented with episodic chest pressure, palpitations, neck tightness, and arm discomfort. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block, and troponin was normal. Exercise stress echocardiography was equivocal, showing 2 mm inferior and inferolateral ST depression without stress induced wall motion abnormality. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed preserved left ventricular systolic function with left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) showed calcium score 0 and a 39 x 39 x 34 mm partially calcified thrombosed aneurysm in the expected left atrial appendage location, supplied by a small left coronary artery, with a normal dominant right coronary artery (RCA). Coronary angiography showed the LM artery terminating into a large aneurysmal mass without antegrade flow into the left anterior descending (LAD) or left circumflex (LCx). Both territories filled retrograde from RCA collaterals. Stress cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) showed moderate inducible ischemia in the anterior, anteroseptal, anterolateral, and distal lateral walls, without infarction or scar. After specialized evaluation, she underwent elective LM aneurysm repair with saphenous vein grafting to the intraaneurysmal LAD ostium and LCx. At follow up, she had returned to work and cardiac rehabilitation with resolution of her symptoms. Discussion: The decision for elective repair was not driven by refractory symptoms or aneurysm enlargement alone. Her symptoms improved with antianginal therapy, and surveillance CCTA showed stable aneurysm size at 6 months follow up. However, angiography demonstrated absent antegrade left coronary flow with LAD and LCx perfusion dependent on RCA collaterals, while stress CMR showed viable myocardium with inducible ischemia in the left coronary territory. In a young active patient, this combination suggested persistent ischemic vulnerability despite clinical stability. Multidisciplinary evaluation therefore favored surgical reconstruction to exclude the aneurysm and restore direct perfusion to the left coronary territory. Conclusion: Giant coronary aneurysms with unusual coronary anatomy require careful multimodality assessment. In this case, integrated CCTA, angiography, and stress CMR clarified the clinical significance of a rare LM aneurysm and guided successful complex surgical repair with favorable early recovery.
nfd646d8fb603: Background New-onset left bundle branch block (LBBB) is the most frequently observed conduction disturbance following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). However, its long-term clinical and functional implications remain incompletely characterized. We performed a contemporary systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the association of post-TAVR LBBB with mortality, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, ventricular function, and permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI). Methods A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar was performed from inception through June 2026 according to PRISMA guidelines. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Randomized, registry-based, and observational studies comparing outcomes after TAVR in patients with and without new-onset LBBB were included. The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included cardiovascular mortality, HF hospitalization or readmission, PPI, and change in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) from baseline to 1 year following TAVR. Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled risk ratios (RR) and mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic. Results Eighteen studies comprising 162,622 patients were included: 28,857 with new-onset LBBB and 133,765 without LBBB. New-onset LBBB was associated with higher 1-year all-cause mortality (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.16-1.48; P<0.00001; I 2 =42%) and cardiovascular mortality (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.23-1.78; P<0.0001; I 2 =26%). Patients with LBBB had a higher risk of HF hospitalization or readmission (RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.19-1.24; P<0.00001; I 2 =0%). The strongest observed association was with PPI, with a more than twofold increase in risk among patients who developed LBBB (RR 2.28, 95% CI 1.67-3.11; P<0.00001). Although baseline LVEF was comparable between groups (MD –1.62%, 95% CI –3.76 to 0.52; P=0.14), patients with LBBB demonstrated a greater decline in LVEF at 1 year (MD –3.12%, 95% CI –4.37 to –1.88; P<0.00001; I 2 =40%), consistent with adverse ventricular remodeling and impaired functional recovery following TAVR. Conclusions New-onset LBBB after TAVR is associated with a distinct high-risk clinical profile characterized by increased mortality, greater HF burden, progressive ventricular dysfunction, and substantially higher rates of pacemaker implantation. These findings suggest that conduction system injury following TAVR may carry clinical consequences that extend beyond the periprocedural period. These findings emphasize the need to develop techniques and TAVR designs that minimize conduction system injury.
n1a7ba0577c7e: Background Despite guideline-recommended antiplatelet therapy, recurrent stroke risk remains high following noncardioembolic ischemic stroke (NCIS). Factor XIa inhibitors, including asundexian and milvexian, selectively target pathological thrombosis while preserving hemostasis, representing a novel antithrombotic strategy. This meta-analysis aims to assess the efficacy and safety of Factor XIa inhibitors for secondary prevention of NCIS. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Cochrane, Scopus, and EMBASE databases up to May 8, 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, comparing Factor XIa inhibitors with placebo in patients with NCIS or high-risk transient ischemic attack. The primary outcome was the incidence of recurrent ischemic stroke, and secondary efficacy and safety outcomes included all-cause mortality, major bleeding, clinically relevant non-major bleeding (CRNM), and intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). Data were extracted and analyzed using random-effects models to calculate risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Three RCTS (N=16501) were included. The pooled analysis showed that Factor XIa inhibitors significantly reduced the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke than placebo (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68-0.86, P < 0.00001; I 2 = 0%). The use of Factor XIa inhibitors did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.85-1.18, P = 0.98, I 2 = 0%). For safety outcomes, there was no significant difference between the two groups for major bleeding (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.89-1.45, P = 0.32; I 2 = 0%), CRNM (RR 1.54, 95% CI 0.89-2.66, P = 0.12, I 2 = 62%), and ICH (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.73-1.70, P = 0.62; I 2 = 0%). Conclusion In conclusion, Factor XIa inhibitors significantly reduce the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke in patients with NCIS. No increased risk of major bleeding, CRNM, and ICH was seen with Factor XIa inhibitors compared with placebo. These findings suggest that Factor XIa inhibitors are a promising class of drugs for secondary stroke prevention in patients with NCIS and also have a stable hemostatic profile.
n38746a6cd08e: Introduction: Tc-99m pyrophosphate (PYP) scintigraphy has transformed the noninvasive diagnosis of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR), often obviating endomyocardial biopsy (EMB). However, false-positive uptake may occur in nonamyloid conditions. We describe a case of longitudinal progression from Perugini grade 0 to grade 3 uptake in a patient with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis (HD), highlighting an important diagnostic pitfall in the evaluation of suspected ATTR. Case Description: A 63-year-old woman with ESRD on hemodialysis, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (EF 60-65%), hypertension, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism was evaluated for suspected cardiac amyloidosis. Two years before presentation, PYP scintigraphy performed prior to HD initiation showed Perugini grade 0 uptake. Baseline echocardiography showed moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) without infiltrative features. Over the ensuing two years, she developed recurrent intradialytic hypotension and atrial fibrillation. Echocardiography revealed severe concentric LVH with interventricular septal thickness of 1.85 cm, dynamic mid-left ventricular cavity obstruction (peak gradient 70 mmHg with Valsalva), and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. EKG showed atrial fibrillation and low-voltage QRS complexes disproportionate to LVH severity. Cardiac MRI demonstrated diffuse late gadolinium enhancement involving the mid-myocardium, epicardium, and posterior right ventricular wall. Repeat PYP scintigraphy with SPECT confirmed Perugini grade 3 uptake (Figure 1). Serum immunofixation was negative, and kappa/lambda ratio was normal. Phosphorus was 7.2 mg/dL, and PTH was 292 pg/mL. ATTR genetic testing was negative. EMB revealed cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, minimal interstitial fibrosis, and no amyloid deposition on Congo red staining (Figure 2). Subsequent mitral valve replacement for significant MR revealed valvular calcification. Discussion: The progression from a negative scan to strongly positive uptake paralleled HD initiation, metabolic derangements, and structural remodeling, suggesting that non-amyloid cardiac processes can mimic ATTR on scintigraphy (Figure 3). Hyperphosphatemia and hyperparathyroidism likely promoted myocardial calcium-phosphate deposition, while chronic mechanical stress, reflected by marked LVH, may have driven fibrosis and microcalcification, providing an additional substrate for tracer uptake. Although EMB showed no calcification, microscopic calcium-phosphate deposits below the resolution of light microscopy cannot be excluded and may account for Tc-99m PYP uptake. This case underscores the value of EMB when significant metabolic or structural confounders accompany a positive scan, thereby preventing misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment.
nf8f88e2356f8: Atrial fibrillation affects approximately 60 million people globally and is associated with a 2-fold increase in cardiovascular mortality. EAST-AFNET 4 showed that early rhythm control reduces major adverse cardiovascular events by 21% compared with rate control, but nearly one in five patients in that trial's rhythm control arm underwent catheter ablation. Whether antiarrhythmic drugs alone confer independent outcome benefit remains unresolved. We sought to quantify the pharmacologic component of this effect in isolation.We performed a systematic review and pairwise meta-analysis of randomized and observational studies comparing antiarrhythmic drug-based early rhythm control, without ablation, versus rate control in atrial fibrillation diagnosed within one year. Primary outcome was a composite of cardiovascular death, stroke, hospitalization for heart failure, or acute coronary syndrome. A random-effects model with REML estimation and Hartung-Knapp adjustment was fitted. Where multiple publications from the same national registry database were identified, the largest non-overlapping cohort per distinct analytic population was retained to avoid double-counting of patients.After applying the registry overlap exclusion rule, 2 studies were retained: Kim et al. (Annals of Internal Medicine 2022; KNHIS general cohort, N=54,216) and Kim et al. (JACEP 2022; KNHIS EAST-AFNET 4-eligible cohort, N=31,220). Three additional Korean NHIS publications were excluded as overlapping subsets of these same two cohorts. Pharmacologic-only early rhythm control reduced the primary composite outcome versus rate control (HR 0.85 [95% CI 0.79-0.92]; P=0.023). Between-study heterogeneity was absent (I 2 =0%; Q=0.08, P=0.78). With k=2, a prediction interval was not estimated.Antiarrhythmic drugs alone, without any procedural rhythm control component, reduce composite cardiovascular outcomes in recently diagnosed atrial fibrillation.
